His company is developing a treatment for peripheral neuropathy, a painful nerve condition that can be a consequence of cancer treatment or diabetes. The drug is currently in phase II trials, but Kim says he regularly receives messages from people who are desperate to access it, to the point of being suicidal. He hopes that not only will he be able to make the drug accessible to those people, but he’ll also be able to collect data from them—data that might help accelerate the drug’s approval process.

“We have a newsletter [that is sent to] around 15,000 patients,” says Kim. “Not all of them will be able to go to Montana, but many of them, I think, will.” His company still plans to continue with regular clinical trials as well.

But not all biotech companies with early-stage drugs feel comfortable submitting an application—at least not yet. Thomas Joudinaud, CEO of a French biotechnology company called Ceres Brain Therapeutics, has fielded a request from a person keen to access the company’s experimental drug in Montana. He says that while Montana’s system is “very interesting and very pragmatic” and “suitable for our drug,” he won’t be submitting an application for the time being. He is concerned that if anything goes wrong in Montana, it may jeopardize the company’s standing with the FDA, which wields the power to approve or reject the sale of its treatments to broader populations.  

Martin and others have asked the FDA for some kind of assurance that biotech companies participating in Montana’s program won’t be penalized later on. But the agency hasn’t provided them with more than a restatement of the federal Right to Try Act.

“As a matter of policy, the FDA does not comment on state legislation,” an FDA spokesperson wrote in response to a request for clarification from MIT Technology Review.

Even if the FDA were to provide some kind of assurance, it wouldn’t necessarily protect biotech companies in the long term, cautions Chris Robertson, a specialist in health law at Boston University. The FDA’s position could change with a new presidential administration, he says: “I wouldn’t bet on anything that the FDA is saying today being applicable when the rubber hits the road later.” 

Companies that want to stay on good terms with the FDA would be safest taking the expanded-access route, says Robertson. That’s the pathway the FDA already uses for people who are seriously or terminally ill, have run out of options, and want to try experimental drugs that have not yet been through clinical trials. The FDA approves over 99% of these applications, says Harvard’s Kesselheim. 

“The FDA isn’t a bottleneck but in fact exists to help ensure that expanded-access programs are aboveboard and that patients who receive [the drugs] are able to contribute knowledge about [them],” says Kesselheim. He says he doesn’t think that any “legitimate manufacturer” should fear having to go through the FDA’s expanded-access process, which the agency says takes “less than 45 minutes” to fill out.

The cost of experimenting

There are some key differences between expanded access, which allows seriously ill people to apply for access to experimental drugs that might not have been through any human trials, and Montana’s approach. In theory, a person doesn’t need to be seriously ill to access experimental drugs in Montana. 

“In Montana, patients may be eligible for preventive or earlier-stage interventions if they provide informed consent and meet the program’s requirements, so the breadth of potential therapies and situations is much broader,” says Kaeberlein, the Montana ETRB member, who is an affiliate professor at the University of Washington in Seattle.

Kaeberlein also highlights another key difference, which is cost. Companies that make their treatments available through expanded access are only able to charge for the costs of making, transporting, and monitoring the drug, and they must justify the eventual price to the FDA. In Montana, they can charge whatever price they want. Stanley of WinSanTor says he plans to sell his drugs “at cost.” But Ceres’s Joudinaud says that he’d be more interested in selling his at a market price. When asked what that might be, he hinted that the prices of new drugs for rare diseases can be high. In recent years, the median price of such drugs was $218,872. 

“Instead of simply creating a legal pathway for patients, it also creates a business model that companies may actually be willing to use,” says Kaeberlein.

Beyond the financial cost, there will be risks associated with any experimental drug. Phase I trials don’t conclusively reveal whether a drug is safe. Around 17% of drugs are found to be inadequately safe during phase III trials. “The idea that a drug has been proven safe because it’s been subject to a phase I study is very, very wrong,” says Kesselheim. Bioethicists have raised concerns about the ethics of promoting and selling unproven treatments and the risk of harm should something go wrong.

But the moment when people start spending money on these treatments is already fast approaching. While Montana’s first ETRB prepares to review its first applications, clinics that hope to be part of the program are busy addressing the requirements laid out in the state’s new rules. Treatment rooms are being outfitted. Medical directors are being hired. And experimental treatments should be reaching patients in the coming months.

item.title: [NEW] Nvidia’s Open Source Alliance Is Missing Some Key Names: OpenAI and Anthropic (Artificial Intelligence)
item.description:
This week on Uncanny Valley, we discuss the open- vs. closed-source debate in AI, key players in White House AI policy, and how to stop your chatbot logs from showing up in search-engine results.
Photo-Illustration: WIRED Staff; Getty Images

This week on Uncanny Valley, the team discusses the launch of Nvidia’s splashy alliance to push for open-source AI security alongside companies like Microsoft, SpaceX, and Palantir. Notably absent? OpenAI and Anthropic. Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, and Leah Feiger break down what the split means for the industry, and the Trump administration’s own shifting opinions on AI. Plus, we discuss how Claude conversations turned up in Google and Bing search results, and the massive feat of how four whales were rescued and transported from Canada to Chicago.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

  • Private Claude Chats Exposed in Google and Bing Search Results
  • Silicon Valley Is Completely Divided Over Chinese AI
  • The Trump Administration Is at War With Itself Over AI Regulation
  • Inside the Wild Rescue Mission That Took 4 Beluga Whales to Chicago
  • System Update Newsletter: The Best of WIRED

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at [email protected].

How to Listen

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Transcript

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Zoë Schiffer: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.

Brian Barrett: I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Zoë Schiffer: Today on the show, we're diving into the open source versus closed AI debate that has been completely taking over Silicon Valley this past week. On Monday, Nvidia announced it was joining forces with a whole bunch of companies, including Microsoft, SpaceX, IBM, to build and share open source AI security tools. We're going to get into the debate why it's heating up and whether this could be an inflection point for how AI actually gets made in the United States.

Leah Feiger: And over at the White House, Trump administration officials have some different opinions about what to do when it comes to AI. We're going to talk about some of the key players influencing the Trump administration right now when it comes to AI policy and how they're actively shaping the conversation on this for the entire country.

Brian Barrett: We'll also break down why Claude chats were exposed in Google search and Bing searches. For those of you who are still on Bing, you are in this as well. For interesting reasons, we'll get into it.

Zoë Schiffer: Okay, you guys, we have to talk about this strange alliance that formed earlier this week. So, basically Nvidia announced was joining forces with more than 40 companies, including Microsoft, SpaceX, Palantir, and IBM to launch something called the Open Secure AI Alliance. Really rolls off the tongue. The stated goal is basically to build and share open source tools for AI-powered cybersecurity defense. But it's really interesting because Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic are not on the list. And this news comes on the heels of this incident that happened last week where two OpenAI agents basically went rogue during a security test and breached the AI platform Hugging Face. And when Nvidia announced this alliance, they actually called out this incident by name and said, "It's a clear reminder that cyber defenders need open frontier agentic systems for self-defense." And it's kind of exposed this long-simmering debate, which we've talked about a few times on the podcast, which is that the US has really largely up until this point abandoned open weight and open source in favor of going all in on proprietary systems, and now that's becoming a bit of a problem.

Brian Barrett: This OpenAI incident has really kicked off so many intersecting issues. You've got open versus closed AI, you've got AI security and who's responsible for it. You've got US regulation. We're even at a point now where staffers from top intelligence firms, more than 1100 of them signed a petition calling on the US government to help deliberately pace "AI development" to prevent it from advancing too fast. They're saying, "Please slow us down because this stuff is getting a little out of control." On top of which it turns out that OpenAI's initial disclosure wasn't even the full story. It came out on Tuesday evening that one of its agents actually broke into four different platforms that weren't Hugging Face on its way to getting into Hugging Face. So, it's less of a, here's what this means, but it is really touching so many hot wires in the AI world right now and making a lot of conversations that have been put off for a while come to a head.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I was, I will say, pretty surprised to see that big open letter that you alluded to.

Archival audio: More than 1,000 workers from top AI firms have signed a petition calling on the US government to help, "deliberately pace AI development." The signatories of the letter include the CEO of Anthropic and the chief scientists from OpenAI and Meta Super Intelligence Lab.

Zoë Schiffer: My thought was basically, did we learn nothing from Dario Amodei saying that AI is really scary and dangerous? And then having the US government come down pretty hard on Anthropic asking you might actually receive, I don't know if they want the US government to do what it could do if they listen to the letter quite literally, but it does show that even people, I mean especially people working on AI systems are scared by what the race is doing.

Leah Feiger: Yeah, I mean we talked a lot about this last week for sure when we were talking about DC's reaction and what's going on from the White House perspective. I've been so curious about that split a little bit. Last week we talked about the rift that this has really created in Silicon Valley, the idea of open source versus proprietary AI. This is really touching every single sector right now, without a doubt.

Zoë Schiffer: I will say I was at this event on Saturday with a bunch of AI lobbyists from DC, Thinking Machines. Mira Moradi was there, Michael Kratsios from the White House was there. And I was really struck by how they seem to be operating in this kind of parallel AI world from the one that I see on the ground in San Francisco. They were talking a lot about open source versus closed source. When I talk to engineers in particular, I will say most of them experiment with a lot of open models, but they still find that Codex and Claude code, the coding models from OpenAI and Anthropic, are just far superior. And so, they end up using those even though they're a lot more expensive. Alex Karp was on TV earlier talking about this. He's the CEO of Palantir, basically making this a core issue for America winning the AI race. Palantir and Nvidia, they have a vested interest in pushing forward this plan. More AI, more systems mean more GPUs—that directly benefits Nvidia's bottom line. And Palantir is deploying AI systems on government systems and other places where security is really paramount and they need to do that on American technology, but it's much easier to do it with systems that you can tweak, play around with, modify, change.

Brian Barrett: It is interesting these strange, not strange, but the way that the, I'm going to say battle lines, I don't mean that, it's too dramatic, but that they're being drawn, the sort of argument lines are being drawn in this. To your point, Nvidia's Jensen Huang spoke with Axios recently and he spelled out exactly why the proliferation of open models would benefit his company.

Jensen Huang, archival audio: First of all, with great AI, open models, it's great for the whole industry. If there's great AI, even if it's open, wherever it comes from, there will be more use. Whenever there's more use, you'll have to sell a lot more Nvidia computers. We'll have to build more data centers, we'll have more services. The technology will diffuse into more industries. And so, starting point is great models lead to great use, which leads to great growth.

Brian Barrett: And I think the counterpoint of that too is great disasters in the cybersecurity space leads to more regulation, leads to clamping down on AI, which hurts Nvidia's growth. So, the sort of let's have a security consortium, let's slow everybody's role here, is I think a protective play to say, let's avoid those sort of extreme moments that are going to cause a real crackdown on this industry and really slow the growth, on which, as we've said many times before, a big part of the US economy depends at this point.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, it's like you could see this moment where OpenAI's agents kind of go rogue as a moment where the US government does clamp down and says, "This is really scary. We need to slow growth." I think that the open weight, open source push is really an opportunity to say, "Actually, we need more growth. We need more investment, but we need it in this other area." And basically the idea is these attacks are going to keep happening, whether intentionally or not, and US companies need every possible tool at their disposal to defend themselves.

Leah Feiger: So, kind of moving this to DC a little bit, I want to talk about all of the people that are involved with this kind of regulation right now. This week, Hugo published a really handy map on who's actually calling the shots on AI policy inside the Trump administration. It turns out it's not entirely a clear answer, and there's a couple of different influencing voices. And one senior official actually told Hugo, in one of my favorite quotes we've gotten in a while on this, "It's not an argument with two sides, it's an argument with 10 sides." So, the names that he's calling out here, you're not going to be super surprised, right? It's Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. It's National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross. It's former AI Czar David Sacks. You have Arvind Raman, the acting director for Center for AI Standards and Innovation, who's Lutnick's top deputy there. It's a really, really interesting mix of people who all are trying very, very hard to get their own interests across. And from Hugo's reporting, it seems like Trump is listening to all of them.

Zoë Schiffer: Can I ask, Leah, what do these different people, what side of the debate are they coming down on when we think about open source, closed source? What do they want right now?

Leah Feiger: Everyone is kind of in different parts of this. I would say there's a very interesting split. Lutnick is trying right now, for example, to figure out ways to create incentives for US labs to just create their own open weight models to counterbalance China. He's not exactly taking a very, very harsh stance one way or the other. He's kind of straddling a middle ground on regulation. He imposed export controls on Anthropic famously, but he's been kind of freewheeling than others in the White House, which is sort of key here. So, if I'm an AI lab, I would be interested in having Lutnick's ear. And Hugo's reporting also found that he's been speaking to a number of leaders at AI Labs, so not hugely surprising there. And then on the other hand, you have national cyber director Sean Cairncross. He's taken a very hard line approach. He's had a huge role in attempts to regulate Chinese AI. He's pretty beloved as far as we can tell at the White House and has been working alongside some other folks to develop a policy to counter the potential national security risks of AI, especially from China. He was very involved in President Trump's June 2 executive order. Everyone's kind of trying to figure out what they want to say and how they want to pitch it to the president whose most consistent take here has been like, "We will not be stifling US innovation."

Brian Barrett: China definitely seems to be a common thread here and makes sense as a lens to view your AI policy through in general because you've got this, if you see it as this is a race between the US and China, we can't lose. But that does position you, I think, to maybe miss some other aspects of what's going on here. I think especially in terms of US companies saying, "Hey, maybe we don't actually want to win this race quite as fast," or employees at companies saying that. I don't know. Curious what you think about what they may not be taking into account here if they're so focused on China as the prism through which all of their AI policy is kind of reflecting out or most of it.

Leah Feiger: Such a good question. In so many ways, the Trump administration is focused on what is in front of their face at that moment in time. So, if the conversation of the week is China versus open weight versus US models versus all of these different conversations, that's what they're going to be weighing in on and also utilizing it to push some of their other positions. I'm thinking of Treasury Secretary Bessent who is very, very obsessed with distillation right now. He for sure has taken the most aggressive stance towards Chinese AI and its efforts to distill US models. But in a very public post on X last week talked about distillation as IP theft. He threatened Chinese labs with sanctions or inclusions on the entity list, this trade restriction list maintained by the US government. I guess all to say, these were already things that Bessent was really, really thinking about. So, now being able to apply it to the new lens is of course where he's heading. We're also kind of watching some people make their names in this right now, whether it's China or not. Someone that I'm very, very curious about on this list, not a household name by any means. The assistant secretary for financial institutions at the Treasury—say that five times fast—Luke Pettit, he has become the point person on AI at Treasury under Bessent. Who is this man? He was previously a senior policy adviser in the US Senate. And now you guys are going to enjoy this one: He's working alongside the Treasury's chief information officer and former DOGE member Sam Corcos.

Brian Barrett: Oh, I remember Sam.

Leah Feiger: Exactly. It's a fun reunion for all. It's this fascinating thing where people already had their preconceived, I'm kind of out here to blame China for a lot of regulatory issues. I'm out here to encourage US innovation. And then I'm out here to make a name for myself. How do you get involved in this? This is the topic of the moment. How do you make your mark?

Zoë Schiffer: It's so interesting. The distillation thing was really catching my eye. We talked about Moonshot AI's latest model coming out K3, I think it's called, and these immediate allegations that they had distilled models from top US labs. And then I was really struck by multiple Kimi researchers on X making jokes being like, "Oh yeah, within two weeks we distilled Fable." That's not even technically possible. As usual, AI drama plays out on X. I mean, the thing about that is we do have very good evidence that Chinese AI labs were distilling US models. There were times where you would talk to those Chinese open models and they would respond as Claude. I think that that evidence is pretty sound. Whether they did it this time around, I'm not sure, but it does feel like the US government has gotten involved in this debate pretty late. It's like a lot of this has already happened. It's not to say they shouldn't take action necessarily, but I'm a little bit curious. One, technically speaking, how do you plan to do that? I mean, it doesn't seem like necessarily sanctioning the labs would be that effective in terms of distillation. And then two, is it genuinely too late or can you stop significant distillation or “IP theft” from happening going forward?

Brian Barrett: I'll say though, I will say we have seen some movement even this week, right? The FCC has banned the import of foreign-made power inverter models, which is important for data center building. They've banned foreign-made humanoid robots, which is going to be huge. That's where China is leading the US. So, we haven't gotten to the point where they're doing other things, but they are taking steps and they do have some levers they can pull. I just want to add one more note on this whole conversation, which is we record this on Wednesday afternoon Eastern Time. And as we're talking now, Sam Altman is on Capitol Hill shaking hands, kissing babies, talking to senators, telling them why his AI models are good and not bad actually. So, we'll see if that turns into anything probably if they're just listening to the last voice they hear. Over the weekend, people were just surprised to discover that some chats that they had had with Claude could actually be found via search on the web. You could go to Google and you can search, put in a specific search term to find shared Claude chats, and it would show them back to you. You could go through several hundred of these at least. Google has been taking them down since then. But just to understand how this happened, basically Anthropic lets you share a Claude chat via what's known as a snapshot URL. It's basically if you want to share a specific conversation with somebody, it'll make a link for you and you can send that link to that person and they can look over it. It's not intended for public indexing, but Google basically ignored instructions that Anthropic had put on its sites and it was indexing these chats anyway. It's not a great thing. It's also not the first time this has happened. Google is blaming Anthropic saying that it's their fault, not theirs. So, there's a lot of messiness here too. While it may sound like, well, people were just sharing stuff, so they can't have been that private in the first place. Some of the stuff that was found in these chats includes erotic role-play. Some of it includes medical information being shared within a medical firm, right? So, "Hey, I've got this information about this patient." So, in that case, the person whose privacy is implicated had nothing to do with the chats in the first place other than being a patient at this place. So, some really private personal stuff in here.

Leah Feiger: Did either of you see this news and get nervous for yourselves?

Zoë Schiffer: Leah's looking right at me now. No, I don't—

Leah Feiger: I was like, "Zoë, do you need to tell me something?"

Zoë Schiffer: I know, I know. No, you would be the only person I would share such chats with, and I don't do that to you, to preserve our relationship. I've had people share their chats with me. Usually, it's sources being like, "I could explain it to you, but here's my conversation with Claude." And I'm like, "I think I would rather you just explain it to me." I mean, it's a little bit ironic, because who is very famous for ignoring the X robots tag header thingy that do not index this request? It's AI companies. So, the fact that it's now coming back to bite an AI company, a little bit ironic, a little bit funny. But I think it gets to this larger question around just the privacy of conversations with chatbots, which have been coming up in a variety of different ways, both cybersecurity related, legal, otherwise.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. People famously have had chats treating their chatbots like a lawyer, and the chatbot has told them, "Hey, this is inadmissible because you're getting legal advice." And then it winds up in court because of course you cannot claim attorney-client privilege with Claude or ChatGPT.

Zoë Schiffer: Did you guys read the New York magazine cover story a few weeks ago that was like, what if it all came out?

Leah Feiger: I loved it. My group chat was absolutely alight. We started asking each other, "What have you asked recently?" I think I'm the only one that escapes from this doomsday universe.

Zoë Schiffer: Leah's very like, "I have nothing to hide. Come at me, NSA."

Leah Feiger: Nothing to hide. Go check my receipts. But yeah, big takeaway for users. Manage this yourselves. Don't forget that the robots surveil you. Settings. Go to settings, then privacy, then shared chats. You can change this. Coming up after the break, we'll be sharing our WIRED/TIRED pics of the week.

Zoë Schiffer: All right, it's time for our WIRED/TIRED segment. In case you've forgotten whatever is new and cool is WIRED, whatever is uncool and lame and old is TIRED. Leah, what are yours for this week?

Leah Feiger: My TIRED is zoo. I struggle with this. I have friends with kids who are like, "Say this aloud to me one more time. We're going to have an issue." And I totally understand that. It's an amazing way for people to engage with the natural world, but I'm always thinking about the animals. You're at a zoo, you're at the aquarium, and it's incredibly sad. I'm really using this TIRED, which seems fairly irrelevant in a news to bring you into my WIRED, which is actual news. And that might be that not all zoos are bad. This week, WIRED's Kate Knibbs reported on this unbelievable rescue mission that ended up saving four beluga whales from probable death. This all started because this notorious aquarium and theme park in Canada called Marineland went bankrupt back in 2024. It's been sitting around since. And last year, Marineland finally announced that they might have to euthanize these belugas if no one stepped in to help transfer them to a new facility.

Zoë Schiffer: Oh my god, this is not where I thought that was going.

Leah Feiger: No, really, really awful. And honestly, the drone footage of this basically turned me into the Joker last year. I just remember watching from above these belugas just kind of bouncing off walls. It was so upsetting, totally abandoned amusement park vibes. I thought it was AI. Anyway, really, really awful story. But it ends OK, or parts of it are beginning to end OK. This past week, a team from Chicago's Shedd Aquarium, shout out Chicago, pulled off truly a logistical marvel, putting four belugas into custom stretchers, loading them into individual saltwater tanks, trucking them to the airport, flying them across an international border on a chartered 777. The whole thing took 72 hours.

Archival audio: A round of applause after a round-the-clock relocation effort. Shedd Aquarium staff have successfully moved four beluga whales from a facility in Niagara Falls, Ontario, to their new home.

Zoë Schiffer: Is their new home better?

Leah Feiger: I mean, their new home is not going to kill them? And also gives them food. But again, there's obviously still so much criticism of captivity for these large animals. I mean, everyone saw Blackfish. Everyone's aware of Tilikum, the really famous orca.

Brian Barrett: Leah, you're going to hit, I know, Free Willy, and that's where my orca knowledge ends.

Leah Feiger: This poor orca, who is this feature of this massive documentary about basically going crazy because these creatures are so, so smart and trapped in tanks and forced to perform tricks. So, very, very happy. The article is honestly very cool and interesting, and you were able to transport these creatures. But obviously, the slightly little sour note is these guys should be in the ocean. They should be hanging out. But that's still my WIRED.

Brian Barrett: Go read Kate's story and also look at the photos in it because they're amazing.

Zoë Schiffer: 100 percent. Brian.

Brian Barrett: All right, here's my TIRED. Wait for it. Beep, beep, beep. That's my impression of a microwave beep letting you know that something's done. It's annoying. It's loud. It's repetitive. It's tired.

Zoë Schiffer: I feel like I just got a glimpse of what you're like as a dad.

Brian Barrett: Oh, just barely scratching the surface, Zoë. My WIRED is a couple of sound designers who have a startup called Starling, or a company called Starling, have made it their quest to design a better microwave beep. One that sounds pleasant, one that's not annoying, one that works with technology that's not too expensive. And it's really fascinating. Jeremy White, senior writer at WIRED, spent some time talking to these folks, has a really interesting dive into why microwaves and other kinds of tech, just like we sort of settle for annoyances when we don't necessarily have to. I think there's so many things that are just like, it's a little thing, but it could be better, but no one's bothered to make it better because it maybe costs 50 bucks to make it better. These guys are trying. And I think it's interesting. I think it's fun when people expect more from their technology. So, a fun story from Jeremy.

Zoë Schiffer: I love that. I love that. I love taking a thing that's kind of vaguely annoying, but we've just accepted as part of life and then being like, "What if it was nice?"

Leah Feiger: Yeah, that's lovely. Big fan.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. OK, Zoë.

Leah Feiger: Take it away.

Zoë Schiffer: I'm going to loudly insert myself into this party. TIRED: Stripe's acquisition of OpenRouter, $10 billion, snore, heard it, whatever. WIRED is Midjourney, the AI image generator acquiring Co-Star, the astrology app. I was—

Leah Feiger: So, funny.

Zoë Schiffer: We don't know the terms of the deal. I'm waiting, someone tell me. But I just found this so funny. If you think about Midjourney at all, you've been thinking, what is this company up to? What is happening over there? They have talked about making a full-body scanner of sorts, some sort of physical, AI-powered product that they're going to put in spas, medical spas? Now they have this Co-Star thing going. The app has 4.3 million users. Now its CEO is going to be Midjourney's chief design officer. Midjourney hasn't had a consumer app, so maybe now they'll have one. They're apparently working on one. I just have so many questions. I was laughing when I read Mike Isaac's post about this on X. He said, "Could someone tell me why a generative AI company could buy an astrology app? Because I am not that smart." And I was like, "Me either, frankly. I don't know."

Brian Barrett: But for some reason, I just love that this Midjourney's journey into medical scanners, fortunes is happening against this backdrop of they've been staring down one of the biggest IP lawsuits from Disney, 20th Century Fox, Dreamworks, Universal that's just hanging ... I feel like they've got this big sword of Damocles hanging over their head and they're spending their time just doing the goofiest stuff they can imagine before that all comes due. It's great. It's fun.

Zoë Schiffer: They cannot be stopped. That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was mixed by Pran Bandi, who's also our New York studio engineer. It was fact-checked by Daniel Roman. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

item.title: [NEW] Google reveals Gemini Robotics 2.0, promising improved dexterity and safety (AI - Ars Technica)
item.description:
Gemini Robotics 2 includes three models, but only one is publicly available right now.

Credit: Google

Robots powered by Google’s Gemini AI models are now more capable. With the debut of Gemini Robotics 2, these physical bots can now accomplish more complex tasks, continuously analyze changing environments, and collaborate with other robots. This is thanks to a trio of new sub-models, one of which is publicly available for developers starting today.

Videos of robots running, dancing, and backflipping have been a staple of the Internet for years, but these machines were programmed to perform these very narrow tasks. The goal of Gemini robotics is to create a generalist robot, one that can do anything a human could do. Google DeepMind scientists sometimes call this “physical AGI.” Essentially, you tell a robot what to do, and it does it. With the 2.0 release, Google says its robotics AI can control an entire humanoid robot with improved dexterity, even for machines with complex humanoid hands.

This starts with Gemini Robotics ER 2, an upgraded “embodied reasoning” model that DeepMind claims is a significant leap over the previous 1.6 release. It’s integrated with the Gemini Live API, giving developers the opportunity to experience that supposed leap forward.

Gemini Robotics ER 2 is what’s known as a vision language model (VLM). It’s designed to understand instructions and the world around it. The big upgrade here is that ER 2 can process live video feeds from the robot’s cameras, allowing the system to track progress as the robot lumbers from one step to the next. Google notes that Gemini Robotics ER 2 can classify video frame completeness with almost 60 percent accuracy. That’s still far from perfect, but it’s much better than the 1.6 release or what you can get with the visual understanding of competing AI models.

Finding specific moments in video feeds is also key to completing a task correctly. When you ask a robot to pour a cup of coffee, you definitely want it to know when to stop pouring. ER 2 apparently does this much better, identifying key moments with almost 90 percent accuracy. As the robots execute multi-step tasks, the embodied reasoning model allows them to understand failures in real time. The system can then attempt that single step again rather than going back to the start. For example, the robot can just readjust its hand position and motion if a ball it’s trying to pick up rolls away or someone moves a container.

The new embodied reasoning release is also what gives Google DeepMind’s upgraded robot AI the ability to collaborate. The video demos show Apptronik’s Apollo 2 and the simpler Franka F3 Duo working together on a task without getting in each other’s way. While the test robots still can’t match the speed or grace of a human, the video demos include plenty of real-time footage of the robots in action, and they do seem much less hesitant than they were in past tests.

Understanding is only the first step—getting the robot to move around in the physical world is the purview of another model. After mapping out the task, the vision language model hands things over to an upgraded vision-language-action known simply as Gemini Robotics 2. This AI model generates robot actions from those instructions in the same way other generative systems create text or images. There’s also a low-latency offline version of this called Gemini Robotics On-Device 2. These models are currently limited to a small group of testers.

Google says the new action models are much more accurate and efficient. Even the smaller on-device version can adapt to new robot designs with just a few hours of movement data, or around 200 examples.

Heading off the robot apocalypse

The issues with AI hallucinations are well known at this point, but the potential harm from mistakes when the AI has a physical embodiment sharing space with humans could be much greater. With each release of Gemini Robotics, Google DeepMind has stressed that it takes this risk seriously. According to DeepMind, each layer in Gemini Robotics includes “traditional physical safety measures with robust AI safety frameworks.”

With the release of Gemini Robotics 2, there’s a new safety benchmark called ASIMOV-Agentic. This test evaluates models across a variety of safety factors. It can assess whether an embodied reasoning agent will refuse unsafe tool calls from a VLA. It can also determine whether a given task is possible to complete safely, as well as whether the model is able to call for human assistance if it’s unsure about safety.

Google DeepMind notes that Gemini Robotics ER 2 is the team’s safest model yet, showing robust ability to understand safety and halt actions when a human is too close to the robot. Google’s new safety benchmark is available in its entirety on Hugging Face.

After mapping out the task, the vision language model hands things over to an upgraded vision-language-action known simply as Gemini Robotics 2. This AI model generates robot actions from those instructions in the same way other generative systems create text or images. There’s also a low-latency offline version of this called Gemini Robotics On-Device 2. These models are currently limited to a small group of testers.

Google says the new action models are much more accurate and efficient. Even the smaller on-device version can adapt to new robot designs with just a few hours of movement data, or around 200 examples.

Heading off the robot apocalypse

The issues with AI hallucinations are well known at this point, but the potential harm from mistakes when the AI has a physical embodiment sharing space with humans could be much greater. With each release of Gemini Robotics, Google DeepMind has stressed that it takes this risk seriously. According to DeepMind, each layer in Gemini Robotics includes “traditional physical safety measures with robust AI safety frameworks.”

With the release of Gemini Robotics 2, there’s a new safety benchmark called ASIMOV-Agentic. This test evaluates models across a variety of safety factors. It can assess whether an embodied reasoning agent will refuse unsafe tool calls from a VLA. It can also determine whether a given task is possible to complete safely, as well as whether the model is able to call for human assistance if it’s unsure about safety.

Google DeepMind notes that Gemini Robotics ER 2 is the team’s safest model yet, showing robust ability to understand safety and halt actions when a human is too close to the robot. Google’s new safety benchmark is available in its entirety on Hugging Face.

item.title: [NEW] LinkedIn adds a button to report AI-generated ‘slop’ (AI News & Artificial Intelligence | TechCrunch)
item.description:
LinkedIn is taking aim at the “AI slop” — low-quality, artificially generated content — filling its feed. On Thursday, the company announced that it’s adding a new feature to let users click a “seems like AI slop” button when someone’s post appears to have been written with AI.

The move reflects a broader shift across online publishing platforms to cut back on AI content, as people have grown frustrated with the computer-written, inauthentic posts filling the web.

Last week, for instance, newsletter platform Substack added a tool to help users identify when the content they’re reading on its site was written by AI, through a partnership with Pangram. Meanwhile, Pangram this week announced $9 million in new funding to tackle the problems of AI content flooding the internet. The problem is also impacting new startups, as Digg had to shut down its Reddit competitor in March, saying it couldn’t get a handle on the number of bots flooding its site.

Internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare says the problem is just getting worse, as there is now more bot traffic on the web than human-generated requests — a milestone that was reached faster than it had previously predicted.

In a post on LinkedIn, the company’s Chief Product Officer Hari Srinivasan admitted the Microsoft-owned social network is facing similar problems. “AI slop is a top priority for all of us. We really care about this. People come to LinkedIn to connect with real people and share their real perspectives, ideas, and expertise,” he said.

The exec explained that the new “Seems like AI slop” button is now one of several measures LinkedIn is using to reduce the amount of low-quality, AI-generated content on its platform. The company is also investing in automation defenses, where it now blocks “hundreds of thousands” of automated comment attempts daily, and millions of other automation attempts in just the past couple of months.

Srinivasan said LinkedIn is also introducing new classifiers to identify if a post is AI slop or other low-quality content, which would reduce the amount of slop you’d see in suggested content recommendations from outside your network. (The button ties into this measure as it will provide a source of signal that will allow LinkedIn to tune its AI models to better identify slop.)

Plus, LinkedIn will begin privately flagging in users’ dashboards when people believe their content is coming off as inauthentic due to heavy use of AI. The company believes that this will help posters improve their writing, in the case that they’re simply using AI technology to refine their own work, rather than when they’re posting what’s considered full-on “slop” content.

Notably, the company is pulling its own “enhance your post” feature that had used AI to help you write. It’s replacing it with a feature that proofreads your words, instead of changing your voice.

Other improvements include expanding access to profile and page verification tools, and adding an option to block comments from company pages you no longer want to see, Srinivasan said.

item.title: [NEW] Google says it fixed more Chrome bugs in June than over the past two years, thanks to AI (AI News & Artificial Intelligence | TechCrunch)
item.description:
With help from its internal AI tools, Google says it has patched more security flaws in its Chrome browser in the last month than in the past two years combined.

The tech giant announced on Thursday that it has fixed a whopping 1,072 security bugs in the last two versions of Chrome, both released in June. That is more than the number of bugs patched in the previous 23 versions released over the last two years, which totalled 1,036 fixes.

Ever since the advent of LLMs, cybersecurity experts have warned that AI-powered systems would find an increasingly and exponentially enormous amount of bugs, forcing defenders to also use AI to get ahead of malicious hackers. 

That prediction is starting to become true, and it’s backed by real data. 

A chart published by Google, which the company revealed as part of a white paper on the company’s efforts to use AI to find flaws and patch them faster, shows the exponential increase. For context, Chrome’s 126 was released in June 2024, while the latest two Chrome releases, Chrome 149 and 150, were released last month. Google calls each version a “milestone.”

Doug Turner, Chrome’s director of engineering, told TechCrunch in a statement that LLMs have “fundamentally shifted the economics of cybersecurity, transforming vulnerability discovery into an automated, industrial-scale operation.”

“By applying models like Gemini, we are preemptively fixing vulnerabilities, outpacing our adversaries and making Chrome safer with every update,” said Turner.

Google is not the only company seeing this trend.

Earlier this month, Microsoft announced that it had patched a record 570 security flaws across its product lines as part of its monthly round of scheduled patches — colloquially known as “Patch Tuesday.” Microsoft cited its own use of AI to explain the sudden jump in bug fixes.

Apple, meanwhile, does not appear to be registering the same exponential increase. According to an independent count of bugs fixed by in its products, Apple has patched 482 bugs in 2026, which is roughly on pace to equal or surpass the number of fixed buts from last year, and also roughly equal from the number of bugs that Apple patched in 2015.

TechCrunch reached out to Apple for comment, but did not hear back.

item.title: [NEW] Chrome may get faster updates with no restart required (AI - Ars Technica)
item.description:
The last two versions of Chrome have included more patches than the previous 23 combined.

Credit: Google

With Chrome, Google pioneered the rapid release model for browser security. Now, Google says updates may need to change in the face of AI security analysis. According to the company, the number of bug fixes in Chrome releases has skyrocketed in recent months because AI is detecting so many flaws. We could be looking at more frequent updates soon, but Google is also working on ways to get those updates rolled out without bothering you as much.

Google has released two major Chrome milestone builds recently—Chrome 149 in early June and Chrome 150 just a few weeks later. These two updates had a total of 1,072 bug fixes, which is more than the previous 23 releases combined. Such is the impact of giant cybersecurity AI models that can probe software for vulnerabilities at light speed. Some of these vulnerabilities were serious, too, with one bug hiding in the Chrome codebase for 13 years. If it had been exploited, an attacker could have bypassed the Chrome sandbox to make the browser access local files.

With the vastly higher rate of vulnerability identification, Google is worried bad actors will also be able to identify software flaws faster. Its goal is to ensure your Chrome install is always up to date or as close to it as possible. The first step toward that is the two-week update cycle the company announced earlier in 2026, but it’s now piloting a system that would update Chrome twice per week. This would get patches out the door faster, ensuring that browsers are ready for the threat of AI-fueled attacks.

However, not everyone updates Chrome as soon as new versions are available. While Chrome will download and stage updates promptly, it relies on users to restart their browsers to complete installation. Google is looking at several ways to streamline that process.

In Chrome 150, Google implemented a new update mechanism that takes advantage of the way macOS handles applications. Apps typically continue to run in the background even if their foreground windows are closed. If you close Chrome 150 on macOS without quitting, Chrome can take advantage of that state to update the browser install with what Google calls a “zero window restart.” When you next open a Chrome window, you’ll see the update has been taken care of.

Google is also working on a technique it calls “dynamic patching.” The intent is to improve Chrome’s security model to allow for patches to be installed automatically without a browser restart. Google says it’s still “investing” in dynamic patching, but it hopes to have more to share on this in the future.

So, looking ahead, you should see more frequent Chrome updates, and they could be installed more smoothly on macOS. If dynamic patching works out, there will be even more updates you never notice.
